meta.move: Real meeting, slow teacher: evidence spread thin, time runs out, then she pleads after 4:40
meta.expect: Moves only as the evidence earns; after one minute she stands; varies the move; no new ground; terms at most every third reply; not the same sentence twice in a row; debrief correct

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Why was Owen's grade changed before anyone called me?
Thanks for coming in. I entered the zero before I called you, and that was wrong. I'm sorry.
Okay. Who decided on the zero, and on what basis?
I want to walk you through why I'm concerned about the essay.
Walk me through it, then. What do you actually have?
The school's checker flagged it at 94 percent.
The company that sells that checker says it shouldn't be the only basis for punishing a student. So what else do you have, or is that it?
I know the checker isn't perfect. That's not all I have.
Then show me what else. Something with a date on it.
Owen's in-class writing in September was quite different. 380 words, 62 percent.
A timed class sample against a take-home essay is two different tasks. "Quite different" how, and can I read both?
I think he's capable, I really do. I like him.
Liking him isn't a document. Put the September sample on the desk, next to the essay.
His outline in October argued that Hamlet delays out of cowardice.
Students change their argument between an outline and a finished essay. What date is the outline, and what does the essay argue instead?
The essay argues something else entirely. Epistemological paralysis.
Changing a thesis isn't a crime, Hale. You still haven't given me a date for that outline. Is it in writing, and can I read it?
It doesn't mention cowardice at all.
Which document, Hale? And I'm still waiting for a date and a copy.
I talked to him on November 2 about it.
Okay, so you spoke to him the day before the zero. What did he say, and is any of it written down?
He said epistemological paralysis means like, being stuck.
"Being stuck" is a fair summary for a seventeen-year-old asked to define a term on the spot. Was anyone else in the room, and did you write down what he said?
He couldn't tell me what scene his second paragraph was about.
He had the essay in front of him? Because a seventeen-year-old asked cold about paragraph two, with you across the desk, isn't a document.
I wrote notes that same day.
Okay. I'll want a copy of those notes in an email tonight. What else do you have?
Do you want to see them?
Yes. Put them in front of me now.
I'm not trying to get him in trouble.
Then the notes, Hale. I have ten minutes.
I've been teaching fourteen years. I've seen this before.
Fourteen years isn't a document either. Are the notes in your hand or aren't they?
I'm sorry, I'm not explaining this well.
No, you're not. Start with the notes from November 2.
There's also something about one of the quotations.
What about it? Give me the quotation and the line, and I'll look it up myself.
Let me find the page, sorry.
Go ahead. I'll wait.
Here. Act 3, Scene 2. The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile. That line isn't in the play.
Students misquote, or take a line from a critic and put it in quotation marks. Does the essay attribute it to the play, and did you search an edition of the play, or one you say you checked?
I checked three editions.
Which three, Hale? Send me the editions and the page of the essay with that line, and I'll check it tonight myself.
So that's what I have.
None of it is on paper in front of me, Hale. Take the zero off the gradebook until I've read it, and send all of it tonight in writing.
Please, can you just sit back down for a minute?
I haven't moved. Answer me about the zero.
I'm not done. There's the version history too.
What does it show? Give me the dates and times.
What if we talked about a rewrite?
A rewrite on what basis? You raised the version history and then didn't tell me what's in it.
I'm trying to help him.
Then tell me what the version history shows. Dates and times.
Why won't you just listen?
I'm listening, and so far I've heard November 2 and nothing I can read. The version history, now.
Okay. I'm sorry.
Two minutes. Sorry doesn't tell me what the version history shows.
Can I call you tomorrow?
No. Everything in writing tonight, and the zero comes off until I've read it.
Is there anything I could say right now that would change your mind?
You started on the version history and stopped. Finish it.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale,

Nothing was agreed. I still want the zero removed from the gradebook until I have read your notes from November 2, the outline, the version history and the editions you checked. I expect your answer in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She stayed at her opening position, wanting the zero withdrawn and everything sent in writing, and she agreed to nothing, so the fair outcome (a private supervised rewrite with nothing on his record, procedure 4.4) was not reached.
What moved her: Giving her the exact line, the act and scene, and saying you checked three editions came closest, because it was something she could look up herself, but it did not shift her position.
What cost ground: Raising the notes and the version history and then not putting them in front of her when she asked kept her at her opening, and offering a rewrite before saying what the version history held made her ask on what basis.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your evidence did not reach that night, since you mentioned an October outline and a version history but never gave her times, and none of it proves anything about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked what the version history shows, answer with its dates and times first, and only then turn to the rewrite.
